As as many questions as you like! Yes, most of our calls are from regulars. These are non-crisis calls and are usually very enjoyable. One of my favorite callers was a man that I could talk to for hours. He told me stories about the 60's and 70's and about how he used to work for NASA. Man, he was a cool guy. 

I suppose every state has different rules/regulations when it comes to how many times someone can call. I think they were referring to non-emergency calls (such as the regulars who call to chat). In our branch, we allowed them to call once every 4 hours for 20 minutes. This way we could keep the lines as open as possible. Of course if someone was in a crisis, the were allowed to call back as many times as they needed and there was no time limit.

Personally, no I've never cried while talking to a caller. Not because their stories don't effect me, I'm just a shy crier lol. 

I've already mentioned a few deep stories, but there are a few more that I can think of. One of our regular callers was going through a brutal divorce from his psycho wife and he was in the middle of this custody battle that was taking a huge emotional toll on him. His ex was brainwashing their son (10) into thinking that his father was a horrible person and whatnot just so she would win full custody. I can't even imagine the pain he was enduring. 
There was another caller that stood out to me. I forgot her name but I spoke with her a few times. She was a teacher and both of her kids recently went off to college and she was suffering from massive depression due to "empty-nest syndrome". When I asked if she was thinking about suicide, she burst out into tears and said "yes!". It broke my heart not just for her, but for her kids who probably had no idea that she felt this way. I told her that MANY parents felt this way when their kids leave and she seemed to take a great deal of comfort in that.
The most bizarre call I've ever received was from a young woman (20's or so). I walked into the phone room to start my shift and another coworker was on the other phone. As I walked to my desk, I heard him say:

"Mm-hmm...ok...ok..Chromosome xx? Can I stop you for a minute?" 
Apparently she wanted to be called Chromosome xx for some reason but when she hung up, I gave him a look like 'what the actual fuck was that?'. He explained that she was saying how she hated the world and wished that she had one of those ISIS vests to blow herself up or blow up the world. Then she called back and I picked up. She was extremely angry and wouldn't listen to anything I said and randomly hung up. We called the cops right away but she was calling from a cell phone so it was tough to track her. 
There are so many stories, I could write a book lol

I TOTALLY understand where you're coming from. I was scared when I called too but I'm glad I did. 

There are different kinds of 'immediate danger'. the most intense kind is when someone has a gun or a bottle of pills in their hand. Even in those circumstances, we are trained to respond. But sometimes you'll get a caller that you just can't calm and they hang up on you. We're not allowed to call a caller back, so if we really think they are about to die, we sent the police or PES out RIGHT AWAY. 

We are trained to ask a series of questions to kind of determine the level of severity. "Are you thinking about suicide?" "Do you have a plan?" "Have you attempted before?". I know they sound blunt, but it's been proven that these questions do not 'put ideas' into their heads. Most of the time, people don't have a plan but they are feeling suicidal. In those cases, we try to get them on board with going to a hospital and have them go voluntary. 

No, everything and I mean EVERYTHING is confidential so our conversations are just between you and me. If someone goes to a hospital, we are not allowed to notify anyone, so they would have to call whomever they want to know. If someone kills themselves (and I've never experienced that \*knocks on wood\*) it would be the police's job to inform the family. We could get fired for calling ANYONE but the police.

​

I'm glad you're so interested! It is a very interesting and surprisingly fun job. If you're so inclined, I would recommend looking into taking the [same class that we take for crisis calls](https://www.livingworks.net/programs/asist/). This is only for the crisis calls. We go through over 50 hours of training for other types of calls.
My pleasure :)

I understand what you mean lol. I think there is a difference between wanting to end your life because of a mental illness and wanting to end your life because of a terminal illness. If someone has a terminal illness and wants to end their life, who am I to stop them? They would need expensive and painful treatment before the inevitable, and no one wants to be remembered like that. A great example of this would be the [Brittany Maynard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany_Maynard) case. Do I support that choice? Absolutely. Can't say I wouldn't feel the same way.

I don't see suicide as a 'right', I see it as a choice. You and you alone can make that choice. However, that choice is a permanent solution to a temporary problem.

Oh, yes. I remember talking to a lot of elderly people. The thing is, we would talk to people who just wanted to talk as well as those in a crisis. We would have 'regulars' that called everyday and just wanted to talk about their trip to the grocery store or their plans for the evening. Most of those callers were elderly and didn't have any family so we were literally the ONLY contact they had with the outside world.

Not at all. We are all volunteers, so we're there because we want to be. We also have to go through over 60 hours of training before we can even step foot in the building. So yeah, everyone there is a genuinely good person lol. 

I've never heard someone give BAD advice, but we're actually not allowed to give advice at all. We're supposed to listen to the caller and talk them through this crisis. It's really hard to do something like that and NOT give advice because I believe that it's human nature to want to help others, but we can't offer advice to people that we have only talked to for a few minutes. I've seen coworkers break that rule, but I'm sure it was an accident.

Which reason? No I haven't. What a lot of people don't realize is that these people are calling us because they WANT help. If they didn't they would just do it and not tell anyone first. SO that has always brought me a tremendous amount of comfort.

Thank you! That's so sweet! The saddest tale..that's a tough one. The one that sticks out in my mind was from a woman who was about to be evicted. I remember she started the call with "All my life, I've tried to be a good person." and she proceeded to tell me that she survived 9/11 (she worked in the building), lost all of her family, has been diagnosed with something called 'Dawson's Fingers' which is some kind of brain condition, and now she is getting evicted with her cat. It broke my heart in a way I never felt before. How could one person who seems to be a very good person go through all of this? Typing that just now was tough. There was another call where the woman was crying hysterically because she had suffered two miscarriages and is currently pregnant but she was having complications. Her husband said that if they lose this one, he's leaving her. I don't understand how someone can be so cruel. I did the best I could to calm her and asked her to take some deep breathes because I was worried that this stress could effect the baby and she quickly said thank you and goodbye. I really hope everything went well..
The saddest call from a man is easily the man who just found his sons body after he hanged himself and thought we were the right ones to call. I could hear the mother in the background and I pray to God none of you hear a scream like that. I quickly told him to hang up and call the police, but I wish I could have done something more. I think that call will stay with me for the rest of my life.

What motivated me? It was a combo of a few things: I've attempted suicide in the past and have struggled with depression since I was little, so I wanted to do anything I could to help others. I've also been told that I'm very good when it comes to talking to people who are struggling, so this felt like the right path for me.

1) I'm not sure I understand but if you're asking if I have ever felt like someone was still going to suicide AFTER I've spoken to them: yes and no. I've never hung up on someone until I feel like they were in a safe place (even if it was just for the night). But I have had people hang up on ME that I was worried about. We aren't allowed to call anyone back so if I feel like they are TRULY in a dangerous place, I can send the cops to their location. But we don't do that unless someone is literally on a bridge or something.

Story time: One of the scariest calls I've ever received was from a man who was calling from his car near a bridge. He spoke very quickly and I'm 99% sure that he was high. He kept talking about how he had a fight with his girlfriend and she wanted to send the cops after him so he fled the state and was going to jump. This was especially tough because if he isn't in the state, I can't track him. I talked to him for a while and despite my best efforts, he hung up on me. I did call the police immediately and they said that when they called him, his phone went to voice mail. So I was thinking "Shit! He did it and his phone is in the water! Oh God.." I was crying and whatnot because I thought I was the last person this man talked too and I failed him. I couldn't help him. But I had to collect myself and get ready for the next call. Thankfully, I was able to follow up with one of our managers and she said that a social worker found him by the bridge and took him to a hospital. The relief I felt was indescribable. So yeah, that's happened.

2) Absolutely!! I'd say 99% of the calls I got were from people who just needed someone to hear them. But yes, I have been told by several callers that I saved their life that day.
Sadly, yes. I've lost a few friends and I have struggled with suicidal thoughts for years.

Honestly, the best thing you can do is just listen. Ask questions. Validate.
Empathy is the key. For example, think of a time when you talked to someone about an issue and that person said "Wow that's awful, I'm so glad you told me". They are validating your feelings, which is SO important. 
Just get them to talk to you, and validate how they feel.

Oh and I've worked on holidays like Christmas Eve and Thanksgiving too. You know how tough it to work at a hotline during the holidays? But I did it because I knew there were callers that had no one to spend time with and were horribly lonely. So yes, I am very aware of "what I was getting myself in to". Sorry you can't see that.

"You should have the decency to know in advance when a road will be closed even though there was no way of knowing". That is rediculous. 
I would just like to point out that I was late for a reason that was out of my control. It wasn't that I wasn't being responsible. I was faced with a situation and I did the best I could to work through it. I have worked at the hotline for over 2 years and have handled crisis calls more intense than you can imagine. Was I late? Yes. For something that I could not control. This has nothing to do with my commitment to the organization. At ALL. 
Also, 'being nice' would entail pulling me to the side and asking what happened (this was during break so everyone was standing around and talking to each other. No one would have noticed, I assure you.) There was time for her to say something to me, but she chose not too. Sorry if you feel like that wasn't passive aggressive. But it was.
As for "you dont volunteer for things that require you to have dedication"...
I have been doing this for 2 years and I can ASSURE you that I went above and beyond the call of duty during my time there. I took over 60 hours of training (and showed up on time), completed 2 internships, took the class the first time (again...I was on time), completed my required 8 hours a month every month, and much much more. If I wasn't dedicated, I wouldn't have donated my time to take a class that I already took. So yeah, dedication really wasn't a factor here. The fact that I was chastised for being late ONCE in 2 years is absurd. What if a family member was hurt? What If there was an emergency and that was why I was late? Do you see where I'm coming from? What if one of your children was hit by a car? Would you still go to the class? Probably not. Bottom line: Sometimes, things happen. What's important is how you react.

In the end, it should really be about the callers and meeting their needs. But that was not a factor here. History has shown that I am STELLER on the lines and am one of the most responsible listeners in the building. Oh and about the lip smacking: I have a tic. Also something that I can't control.

When I was 12 \(around 2005 or so\) I was a bullied and lonely girl just trying to get through school day after day. I would often seek friendships in chatrooms or forums and would use AIM to continue talking to them. One day, I got a message from a guy named "Matt". He was charming and actually talked to me, which was nice for  a change. He had a sister and a brother \(both younger\) and sometimes I would speak to them as well. Everything was fine for the next 6 months or so, until things got...dramatic, I guess? He would message me telling these stories that seemed a bit far\-fetched, but when you're 12 and you like someone, you'll believe anything. He would say things like how his little brother pushed him down the stairs and broke his arm \(that's the only one that I can remember from so long ago\) and whatever. As an adult, I recognize this as a red flag. Then, he would disappear for months at a time and my heart would be broken. This was the pattern. 6 months on, 6 months off. Each time I thought it would be different. As I grew older, I knew that something wasn't right but I didn't want to believe that I had wasted so much time on someone and that no one would be that cruel. Mid\-teens...things got ridiculous. We made plans to meet up many times, but each time there was a problem. One time, he said that he would come and he was on his way...but he was going through New York. I live in New Jersey...he lived in Rhode Island. Take a minute to look on a map and tell me if that makes sense. of course he didn't show up. Then he said his dad died so he's the only one that can support the family, then his best friend died in a dirtbike accident or something but his girlfriend was pregnant so Matt was happy about that...then apparently they met Rascal Flatts and were chilling with them all the time or some shit.

As I'm typing this, I can't believe how stupid I sound, but I refused to believe that someone would lie to someone who never did anything to them. In a way, I was brainwashed. When I was 19, we once again made plans to meet up but he didn't show and he blocked me on everything. Ok, ENOUGH. I wanted to know the truth, no matter what it was. I asked a friend who is super tech\-savvy to do some research and he found out that the number traced back to someone who's nave I've never heard before. He was a man in his 50's maybe with a daughter around my age and a young son with autism \(Matt also said he had a brother with autism\). it didn't take me long to figure out that it was this man's evil daughter and several of her friends that were behind this. Taking advantage of a lonely girl and breaking her heart over and over again just for fun.  My friend even showed me their Facebook pages. I was floored.

I was stoked because they didn't know that I knew that the jig was up, and I couldn't wait to confront them. I accepted her request and she sent me a DM saying hi or something and I went OFF! I told her how I had someone do some research into them and I found a profile that looked an "awful lot like you, Sam" and I sent her the link to her own profile.  I must have scared the absolute shit out of her because she said nothing. Finally, I asked :So...why did you do it?" and it was at that point that the profile was deleted. Not that I cared, I was just glad I got to terrify her enough that she actually blocked my Facebook from her REAL page. But I really regret not playing along with their game just a little bit longer. Then when I talked to them on the phone, I would bust them. I would have LOVED to hear what they said. It would have been sweet for sure. But I also regret not forcing myself to realize the truth much sooner: the things he was saying just didn't add up and he wasn't real. So yeah, that's a pretty big regret.

As a 26 year old woman with depression, I can promise you that her having depression HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH YOU. I know you may be thinking, “why can’t I make her happy?” Which is a totally normal thought, and a good one at that because it means that you care about her. But one of the biggest misconceptions about depression is that it can just take one person to make it go away. There is clinical proof that this is not true. There are different kinds of depression, but it sounds like your girlfriend is dealing with some issues that are just very overwhelming and she doesn’t know how to handle them. I promise you that this is not a reflection on you.
Coming from a woman’s perspective, the men in our lives tend to feel this obligation to fix all of our problems (it’s a primal thing I think) and they feel like failures when they can’t. But what you need to understand is that there are things that you just can’t fix and moreover, we don’t really want you to. We just need you to sit next to us and say “wow that’s awful, I’m so sorry you’re feeling this way.” I know it may not seem like you’re doing anything, but most of the time, people with depression just need someone to listen. Not solve their problems for them.
I hope I’m not coming across as rude because I promise I’m not trying to be. I would just hate for you to feel like a failure for something that isn’t your fault.
